title: Light, renewed daily (Isaiah 45:7)
hook: the first blessing praises God who forms light and renews creation every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barchu, the call that a whole room answers. Your line was answer the call. Whose call did you return? Today, the first blessing after the call. Day five hundred sixty-two.

There's a verse from Isaiah that the prayer book borrows, and then quietly changes by one word. That's unusual. The verse comes straight from the prophet, God speaking: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil. The rabbis wanted it for the first blessing before the morning Shema. But they didn't want the word evil in a morning blessing. So they swapped it. Today, the blessing that greets the daylight, and the word that was changed.
screen: `A VERSE FROM ISAIAH.` → `ONE WORD CHANGED.` → `THE BLESSING THAT GREETS DAYLIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, Isaiah forty-five reads: "I form the light, and create darkness; I make peace, and create evil; I am the LORD, that doeth all these things." The morning blessing begins: blessed are you, yotzer or, who forms light and creates darkness, who makes peace and creates all things. Evil became all. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, notices the change and gives a reason: it's a more graceful way to say it. The meaning holds, because all includes everything, but the morning doesn't open with the word evil on your lips. Notice also that the blessing over daylight mentions darkness. The Talmud says that's deliberate too: you mention night in the day, and day at night. Then comes the line that gives today its carry. God, the blessing says, in his goodness renews every day, continually, the work of creation. Hamechadesh. Renews. Not created once, long ago, and left running like a clock. Made new, today. Some Hasidic teachers later pressed the idea further: if creation is renewed continually, then it's renewed every moment, and nothing simply carries on by itself. Whatever you make of that, the blessing's picture is plain. Each sunrise isn't a rerun. It's the world being given again. The light coming through your window this morning is, in this prayer's language, a new act.
screen: `I FORM THE LIGHT, AND CREATE DARKNESS.` · `EVIL BECOMES ALL.` · `NIGHT MENTIONED IN THE DAY.` · `HAMECHADESH: RENEWED EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `CREATION RENEWED DAILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the light. Settle, and breathe. Find the nearest light: a window, a lamp, a patch of sun on the floor. Look at where it falls. Notice its color: white, gold, gray. Notice the shadows it makes, and how they have edges. Then imagine this light didn't exist a moment ago and has just been given, new, for you to see by. If you pray, you can say yotzer or, who forms light. If not, simply watch it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Yotzer Or. Who forms light: the first blessing before the morning Shema, praising a creation renewed every day.
Your line: creation renewed daily. Today, treat one familiar thing, your street, your coffee, a person you live with, as if it was given to you new this morning. Day five hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Yotzer Or is the first of the blessings before the Shema in the morning service, said right after Barchu; on Shabbat and festivals it is expanded with additional hymns.

fork.setup: you're composing the first blessing of the morning from Isaiah's verse: I make peace, and create evil. what do you do with the word evil?
fork.reveal: the rabbis changed it to creates all things. the Talmud says it's a more graceful way to say it, without losing the meaning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pleasant blessing about sunshine.
what it means: each morning the world is given again, and the blessing chooses its words with care.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 11b explains bore et hakol in place of bore ra as lishna ma'alya, a refined phrasing, and requires mentioning night by day.

notes: Isaiah 45:7 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Berakhot 11b: 'creates all' instead of 'creates evil' as lishna ma'alya; and mentioning night by day (midat laylah bayom); confirm both are in 11b.
Hasidic teaching on continual renewal (Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah, citing the Baal Shem Tov) attributed to 'some Hasidic teachers'; confirm.
Shabbat/festival expansions (e.g. Hakol Yoducha, El Adon) mentioned in howItsDone generally; confirm.
